items.a_text: More than twenty different notions of algorithmic fairness have been proposed in recent years.
items.b_text: There is a scarcity of suitable educational materials on aspects of algorithmic fairness.
items.explanation: The claims address different aspects of algorithmic fairness—one regarding the multiplicity of formal definitions and the other regarding educational materials—neither supporting nor contradicting each other.

items.a_text: Outcome control improves perceived fairness by enabling users to recognize algorithmic limitations and reallocate goods to fit their specific contexts.
items.b_text: Individuals tend to perceive algorithms as fairer when the algorithmic decision yields a outcome that directly benefits them.
items.explanation: Both claims address factors influencing perceived algorithmic fairness, but Claim A focuses on user control over outcomes while Claim B focuses on the personal favorability of the outcome.

items.a_text: Racial differences in false positive rates for COMPAS persist across prior criminal record count subgroups among defendants charged with misdemeanor offenses.
items.b_text: Gender-blind COMPAS scores overstate recidivism risk for women compared to men with equivalent criminal histories.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses racial disparities in COMPAS false positive rates, whereas Claim B focuses on gender-based overestimation of recidivism risk, making their findings distinct.

items.a_text: Data preprocessing choices impact the reported fairness measures of fairness-aware machine learning algorithms.
items.b_text: Fairness-enhancing mechanisms in machine learning can be categorized into pre-process, in-process, and post-process mechanisms.
items.explanation: Claim A discusses the empirical impact of preprocessing choices on fairness measures, whereas Claim B presents a conceptual taxonomy of fairness-enhancing mechanisms.

items.a_text: Using a balanced sensitive attribute distribution in adversarial training improves fairness metrics across all tested measures compared to an unbalanced distribution.
items.b_text: Adversarial debiasing on the UCI Adult Dataset reduced predictive accuracy slightly from 86.0% to 84.5%.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses the impact of sensitive attribute distribution on fairness metrics in adversarial training, whereas Claim B reports the effect of adversarial debiasing on predictive accuracy on a specific dataset.

items.a_text: Actual predictions made by different fairness-enhancing algorithms vary significantly from one another.
items.b_text: Predictions made on preprocessed (de-biased) data are rated as fairer than those made on raw data.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses the prediction variability among different fairness-enhancing algorithms, while Claim B focuses on human perception of fairness regarding preprocessed data versus raw data.

items.a_text: The proposed learning algorithm achieves individual fairness by treating similar individuals similarly.
items.b_text: Actual predictions made by different fairness-enhancing algorithms vary significantly from one another.
items.explanation: Claim A asserts that a specific proposed algorithm achieves individual fairness, whereas Claim B observes that different fairness-enhancing algorithms produce significantly varying predictions.

items.a_text: The UA framework unifies prior attempts at formalizing algorithmic fairness.
items.b_text: Fairness definitions across existing literature can be organized into a notationally consistent catalog.
items.explanation: Both claims address the unification and organization of existing fairness definitions, but one claims a specific framework unifies formalizations while the other asserts that definitions can be organized into a notationally consistent catalog.

items.a_text: Outcome explanation produces mixed effects on perceived fairness, increasing it in some contexts and decreasing it in others.
items.b_text: Interactional justice perceptions are higher when an AI makes a positive decision compared to when a human makes a negative decision.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses the mixed effects of outcome explanations on perceived fairness, while Claim B compares interactional justice based on decision outcome valence and agent type.

items.a_text: Training the adversarial head on low-income examples (<=50K) most effectively reduces the equality gap for the low-income label class.
items.b_text: Applying the Reweighing pre-processor on the Adult dataset test partition reduces the statistical parity difference from -0.2021 to -0.0119.
items.explanation: The two claims evaluate different fairness interventions and metrics, so they neither support nor contradict each other.

items.a_text: A majority of survey respondents judged five of the ten evaluated COMPAS features as unfair to use for predicting criminal recidivism risk.
items.b_text: Predictions on cases exhibiting disparate impact are rated as less fair than those on non-impacted cases.
items.explanation: Both claims address human perceptions of fairness in algorithmic decision-making, but Claim A focuses on specific COMPAS features while Claim B evaluates the effect of disparate impact on prediction fairness ratings.

items.a_text: Techniques optimizing for one fairness measure often perform well on different fairness measures.
items.b_text: There is no clear agreement on which fairness definition to apply in each situation.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses how optimization techniques transfer across different fairness metrics, while Claim B concerns the lack of consensus on selecting appropriate fairness definitions for specific contexts.

items.a_text: Training the adversarial head exclusively on negative target class instances (Y=0) theoretically enforces equality of opportunity for the negative class.
items.b_text: Cross-entropy adversarial loss biases the adversary toward predicting the majority class when the sensitive attribute is imbalanced, failing to maximize test discrepancy.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses how restricting the adversary to negative target class instances enforces a specific fairness metric, whereas Claim B focuses on how sensitive attribute imbalance affects cross-entropy adversarial loss.

items.a_text: Data preprocessing choices impact the reported accuracy measures of fairness-aware machine learning algorithms.
items.b_text: Fairness-enhancing mechanisms in machine learning can be categorized into pre-process, in-process, and post-process mechanisms.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses how data preprocessing impacts accuracy evaluation, while Claim B presents a taxonomy for categorizing fairness-enhancing mechanisms.

items.a_text: Optimal equalized odds derived predictors can be constructed from learned binary predictors using linear programming post-processing.
items.b_text: The optimal objective value of the equalized odds adversary upper-bounds the equalized odds distance of any classifier learned from the representation.
items.explanation: The claims address different methodologies for achieving equalized odds, with one focusing on post-processing via linear programming and the other on adversarial bounds in representation learning.

items.a_text: An optimal equalized odds predictor can be derived directly from the Bayes optimal regressor and the protected attribute.
items.b_text: A predictor is counterfactually fair if its distribution over possible predictions for an individual remains unchanged under a counterfactual intervention on protected attributes.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses the derivation of an equalized odds predictor, whereas Claim B defines counterfactual fairness, describing two different fairness constructs.

items.a_text: Techniques optimizing for one fairness measure often perform well on different fairness measures.
items.b_text: More than twenty different notions of algorithmic fairness have been proposed in recent years.
items.explanation: Claim A discusses the performance of optimization techniques across different fairness metrics, whereas Claim B simply notes the number of fairness definitions that have been proposed.

items.a_text: Conservative users perceive the inclusion of sensitive features like gender and race in algorithmic decision-making systems as fairer than liberal users do.
items.b_text: Sensitivity-based explanations significantly lower perceived fairness on disparately impacted cases specifically among individuals who consider using the race feature to be unfair.
items.explanation: Claim A examines how political ideology influences perceived fairness of sensitive feature inclusion, whereas Claim B focuses on how sensitivity-based explanations affect fairness perceptions among individuals opposed to using race as a feature.

items.a_text: A person's assessment of eight latent properties of a feature accurately predicts whether they will judge the feature's use in algorithmic decision making as fair with over 85% accuracy.
items.b_text: Predictions on cases exhibiting disparate impact are rated as less fair than those on non-impacted cases.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses how feature-level latent properties predict fairness judgments, while Claim B focuses on how case-level disparate impact affects perceived fairness, making them distinct findings about fairness perception.

items.a_text: A manifestly fair and uniquely optimal predictive algorithm can violate statistical fairness criteria even when base rates are equal across groups.
items.b_text: Statistical parity is inconsistent with the conjunction of balance for the positive class and balance for the negative class when two groups have unequal base rates.
items.explanation: The claims discuss trade-offs involving statistical fairness criteria under different conditions, specifically equal versus unequal base rates across groups.

items.a_text: Penalizing group fairness violations results in heterogeneous effects on measures of fairness in calibration and cross-group ranking across experimental conditions.
items.b_text: The proportional contribution of between-group unfairness to overall individual unfairness increases as sensitive feature groups are refined through intersectionality.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses the trade-offs of penalizing group fairness on calibration and ranking, while Claim B examines how intersectional group refinement affects the ratio of between-group to individual unfairness.

items.a_text: On the UCI Adult Dataset with adversarial debiasing, false negative rates across female (0.0647) and male (0.0701) subgroups showed no statistically significant difference (p = 0.62).
items.b_text: Applying the Reweighing pre-processor on the Adult dataset test partition reduces the statistical parity difference from -0.2021 to -0.0119.
items.explanation: The claims evaluate different debiasing methods (adversarial debiasing vs. reweighing) and different fairness metrics (false negative rate parity vs. statistical parity difference) on the Adult dataset.

items.a_text: A person's assessment of eight latent properties of a feature accurately predicts whether they will judge the feature's use in algorithmic decision making as fair with over 85% accuracy.
items.b_text: Conservative users perceive the inclusion of sensitive features like gender and race in algorithmic decision-making systems as fairer than liberal users do.
items.explanation: Claim A focuses on predicting fairness perceptions based on feature properties, while Claim B addresses how user political ideology influences fairness perceptions of sensitive features.

items.a_text: Training the adversarial head exclusively on positive target class instances (Y=1) theoretically enforces equality of opportunity for the positive class.
items.b_text: Cross-entropy adversarial loss biases the adversary toward predicting the majority class when the sensitive attribute is imbalanced, failing to maximize test discrepancy.
items.explanation: Claim A discusses how conditioning adversarial training on positive instances targets equality of opportunity, while Claim B addresses how sensitive attribute imbalance affects cross-entropy adversarial loss.

items.a_text: Training the adversarial head on high-income examples (>50K) most effectively reduces the equality gap for the high-income label class.
items.b_text: Applying the Reweighing pre-processor on the Adult dataset test partition reduces the statistical parity difference from -0.2021 to -0.0119.
items.explanation: The claims discuss different bias mitigation techniques (adversarial training vs. reweighing) and evaluate different fairness metrics.

items.a_text: Adversarial debiasing on the UCI Adult Dataset reduced predictive accuracy slightly from 86.0% to 84.5%.
items.b_text: Reject option classification substantially improves fairness metrics on the Adult dataset but causes a significant reduction in classification accuracy.
items.explanation: The claims describe the accuracy impacts of two different fairness interventions (adversarial debiasing versus reject option classification) on the Adult dataset.

items.a_text: Statistical criteria of algorithmic fairness, except calibration, are not necessary conditions for fairness.
items.b_text: Statistical parity is inconsistent with calibration within groups when two groups have unequal base rates.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses whether statistical criteria are necessary conditions for fairness, whereas Claim B states a mathematical impossibility theorem regarding the simultaneous satisfaction of statistical parity and calibration.

items.a_text: Individuals tend to perceive algorithms as fairer when the algorithmic decision yields a outcome that directly benefits them.
items.b_text: An individual's prior trust in machine learning systems positively correlates with their overall perceived fairness ratings of model predictions.
items.explanation: Both claims address factors influencing perceived algorithmic fairness, but one focuses on outcome favorability while the other focuses on prior trust in machine learning systems.

items.a_text: Training the adversarial head on data containing both positive and negative target label classes (Y=1 and Y=0) theoretically enforces demographic parity in predictions.
items.b_text: Cross-entropy adversarial loss biases the adversary toward predicting the majority class when the sensitive attribute is imbalanced, failing to maximize test discrepancy.
items.explanation: Claim A describes a theoretical condition for enforcing demographic parity through target label classes, whereas Claim B identifies a specific failure mode of cross-entropy loss under imbalanced sensitive attributes.

items.a_text: Formal mathematical definitions of algorithmic fairness can be categorized into two broad families: those constraining decision effects on disparities, and those constraining protected characteristic effects on decisions.
items.b_text: It is mathematically impossible to simultaneously fulfill all group-level mathematical definitions of fairness.
items.explanation: Claim A categorizes mathematical definitions of fairness into two conceptual families, while Claim B states an impossibility result about simultaneously satisfying all group-level definitions.

items.a_text: Any constant regressor exactly minimizes all of the proposed fairness regularizers.
items.b_text: A classifier achieves zero individual unfairness under a zero-normalized inequality index if and only if a classifier achieves zero empirical prediction loss.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses constant regressors minimizing fairness regularizers, whereas Claim B connects zero individual unfairness under a specific index to zero empirical prediction loss.

items.a_text: An optimal equalized odds predictor can be derived directly from the Bayes optimal regressor and the protected attribute.
items.b_text: The optimal objective value of the equalized odds adversary upper-bounds the equalized odds distance of any classifier learned from the representation.
items.explanation: The claims address different theoretical properties of equalized odds—deriving post-processing predictors versus bounding distance in adversarial representation learning—without supporting or contradicting each other.

items.a_text: No single fairness-aware algorithm consistently dominates across both accuracy and fairness measures.
items.b_text: Fairness mitigation methods that achieve demographic parity can result in unfairness with regard to equality of opportunity or odds.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses the lack of a universally optimal algorithm across accuracy and fairness metrics, whereas Claim B addresses trade-offs between different mathematical definitions of fairness.

items.a_text: Explanations for decisions made by algorithmic decision-making systems increase user perceptions of fairness in news recommender systems.
items.b_text: Sensitivity-based explanations significantly lower perceived fairness on disparately impacted cases specifically among individuals who consider using the race feature to be unfair.
items.explanation: The claims examine different types of explanations and contexts, with Claim A focusing generally on news recommender systems and Claim B focusing on sensitivity-based explanations in disparately impacted cases.

items.a_text: Demographic parity and equal opportunity cause active harm to a protected group when applied over-eagerly in settings where the protected group proportion is small.
items.b_text: A manifestly fair and uniquely optimal predictive algorithm can violate statistical fairness criteria even when base rates are equal across groups.
items.explanation: The claims discuss different aspects of algorithmic fairness, with Claim A focusing on the potential harm of enforcing fairness constraints in small protected groups and Claim B focusing on optimal algorithms violating statistical criteria despite equal base rates.

items.a_text: Outcome control consistently improves perceived fairness in algorithmic goods division.
items.b_text: Perceived fairness of algorithms has a significant positive impact on satisfaction with algorithmic systems.
items.explanation: Claim A focuses on an antecedent that increases perceived fairness, whereas Claim B focuses on a downstream consequence of perceived fairness on user satisfaction.

items.a_text: The reject option of probabilistic classifiers can be exploited to reduce discrimination in classification.
items.b_text: Data discrimination can be significantly reduced at a small cost in classification accuracy.
items.explanation: Claim A describes a specific technique using the reject option to reduce discrimination, while Claim B states a general trade-off regarding the impact of discrimination reduction on classification accuracy.

items.a_text: Individual fairness is generally more costly in terms of accuracy loss than group fairness across most studied datasets.
items.b_text: Penalizing group fairness violations results in heterogeneous effects on measures of fairness in calibration and cross-group ranking across experimental conditions.
items.explanation: Claim A compares the accuracy cost of individual versus group fairness, while Claim B discusses the varied impacts of group fairness penalties on calibration and cross-group ranking metrics.

items.a_text: Organizations often lack the knowledge and capacity required to identify emergent fairness issues in complex sociotechnical systems.
items.b_text: The concept of algorithmic fairness was largely unfamiliar to participants from marginalized populations.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses organizational knowledge regarding fairness issues, whereas Claim B focuses on the familiarity of marginalized populations with algorithmic fairness.

items.a_text: The term fairness as used in machine learning is best understood as a placeholder for a variety of distinct normative egalitarian considerations.
items.b_text: Social perspectives on algorithmic fairness frequently treat technical fairness approaches as a black box without analyzing specific technical operationalizations or trade-offs.
items.explanation: Claim A addresses the conceptual nature of the term fairness in machine learning, whereas Claim B focuses on how social perspectives treat technical fairness approaches, representing distinct aspects of fairness research.
